questions.q: What is the programme mainly about?
options: How to make a good first impression at work
How we judge people by their faces, often wrongly
The history of the Boston Symphony Orchestra
questions.why: Rob says they're talking about first impressions and how they're often wrong.

questions.q: What kind of faces were rated as more trustworthy in Todorov's tests?
questions.why: Neil says faces that look happy and feminine were rated as more trustworthy.

questions.q: How were more masculine faces seen?
questions.why: Rob says faces that were more masculine were seen as more dominant.

questions.q: What important point does Todorov make about these judgements?
options: They take a long time to form
questions.why: Rob says Todorov's key point is that these judgements aren't accurate.

questions.q: Which judgement best predicts who will win an election, according to Todorov?
questions.why: He says 'the judgement that is most predictive of who is going to win the election is perceived competence'.

questions.q: Which voters are most likely to be influenced by a politician's appearance?
options: Voters who know a lot about politics
Voters who know less about politics
questions.why: Rob says it applies especially to people less educated about politics, around 25% of voters.

questions.q: According to Todorov, what CAN a face tell us?
options: Whether someone is tired or sick
questions.why: Faces carry information about mental state and whether someone is tired or sick, but not character.

questions.q: Why does Neil mention the Boston Symphony Orchestra?
options: To show that not seeing people can reduce unfair judgements
To show that men are better musicians than women
To give an example of a job interview that went badly
To explain why orchestras are so popular in the USA
questions.why: After 'blind auditions', where they didn't see musicians, around 50% of those selected were women.
